newsitem.title: DUBAI: FEATURE-In Saudi, issue is power, not succession.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE-In Saudi, issue is power, not succession.

text.p: Saudi Arabia's Defence Minister Prince Sultan often appears on state television donating multi-million dollar medical centres, or delivering pep talks at military academies.
He works the crowds with a warm smile and walks with an entourage of reporters.

Crown Prince Abdullah's television appearances are usually limited to his weekly majlis, or traditional gathering, where ordinary Saudis line up inside a Jeddah palace to kiss his shoulder in respect and hand him written requests.
The crown prince is destined to lead Saudi Arabia after his half-brother, King Fahd. And Prince Sultan will become heir to the throne, according to tradition.
But in Saudi Arabia, the question is not who reigns, but who rules, diplomats and analysts say.
King Fahd suffered a stroke last November. He temporarily handed the reins of power to Crown Prince Abdullah while he recovered, ending speculation over the succession.
Seven weeks later the Saudi monarch resumed his duties, but many Saudis are still pondering their fate, analysts say.
Western diplomats and analysts say Prince Sultan is manoeuvering to gain more power while King Fahd is still at the helm of the world's biggest oil producer and exporter.
"Prince Sultan is very active. He wants to spread his influence. He recently held a meeting with businessmen in Jeddah. He wants to show he's not only defence minister," said a Saudi analyst.
Prince Sultan has poured millions of dollars into humanitarian causes in the kingdom and started a charity foundation in his name.
He also seems sensitive to the new political climate in the kingdom.
Saudi Arabia, traditionally an island of stability in the volatile Middle East, was rattled by two bombings that killed 24 Americans in the last year.
Moslem militant groups who condemn Riyadh's close ties with Washington have been blamed for at least one of the blasts and have threatened more violence.
Prince Sultan, widely seen as pro-American, appears to be projecting a new message in Saudi Arabia, where analysts say anti-American sentiments are also spreading to other quarters.
He recently said there were no American forces in Saudi Arabia, stressing that the 5,000 U.S. military personnel in the kingdom were tied to United Nations resolutions.
One week earlier he said that, if asked, Saudi Arabia would have refused to give the United States access to its bases for recent missile strikes against Iraq.
"During the Gulf War, Abdullah was very quiet. He didn't like the presence of all the U.S. troops in the kingdom. This earned him a lot of respect," said a Western diplomat.
"Now Sultan is trying to project a similar image. He recently made comments about U.S. forces in the kingdom as a way of trying to stake out new territory," he added.
Prince Sultan is a full brother of King Fahd. Crown Prince Abdullah, the austere heir apparent to the throne, has the handicap of being a half brother in the Saudi royal family.
Full brothers and their sons usually back each other when making crucial decisions in the desert kingdom, ruled by the al-Saud family for more than half a century.
But Crown Prince Abdullah's serious reputation and tribal followers have earned him unparalled respect, diplomats say.
He also enjoys the loyalty of the tribal-based, well-armed 57,000-man National Guard, described by a Western diplomat as "one of the most plausible fighting forces in Saudi Arabia".

Crown Prince Abdullah became commander of the mainly U.S.-trained National Guard in 1962. It is charged with defending the kingdom's strategic installations, including oil producing and exporting facilities.
He is seen as less pro-Western than both King Fahd and Prince Sultan. Diplomats say he is also viewed as a devout figure, a key trait in one of the world's most conservative Moslem states.

The analysts and Western diplomats said the six full brothers of King Fahd, unhappy with the prospect of Crown Prince Abdullah on the throne, had put pressure on the Saudi monarch to resume his duties.
But Western diplomats do not expect any rivalries to undermine a smooth succession.

"At this juncture al-Saud realise any sort of split means they will all go crashing down. They all realise the need for a smooth succession. More than anything else they want a measure of stability," said one diplomat based in Riyadh.
